title: Quinoa: Protein, Fiber, and Nutrition

seo.title: Quinoa: Protein, Fiber, and Nutrition
seo.meta_description: Cooked quinoa provides about 120 calories, 4.4 g protein, and 2.8 g fiber per 100 g. Dry quinoa looks much more concentrated because it contains less water.
seo.search_intent: Understand quinoa nutrition and the difference between dry and cooked values.

excerpt: Cooked quinoa provides about 120 calories, 4.4 g of protein, 21 g of carbohydrate, and 2.8 g of fiber per 100 g in USDA reference data. Dry values are much higher per 100 g because the grain has not absorbed cooking water yet.
content_html:
Quinoa is often marketed for protein, but its nutrition is broader than one number. It is a carbohydrate-rich pseudocereal with more protein and fiber than many cooked refined grains, plus minerals such as magnesium, phosphorus, and iron.

A useful reference: 100 g cooked

USDA FoodData Central lists cooked quinoa at roughly 120 calories, 4.4 g protein, 21 g carbohydrate, 1.9 g fat, and 2.8 g fiber per 100 g. A cooked cup around 185 g provides roughly 8 g protein.

That is meaningful for a grain-like side dish, but it does not match cooked lentils, which commonly provide more than 8–9 g protein per 100 g.

Why dry quinoa looks much higher in protein

Dry quinoa is around 14 g protein per 100 g because it contains far less water. Cooking adds water and increases weight, so the protein becomes distributed through a larger mass.

The amino-acid profile is a strength

Quinoa contains all essential amino acids and is relatively rich in lysine compared with many cereal grains. That describes protein quality, not an unusually high total protein content.

Fiber and minerals

At roughly 2.8 g fiber per 100 g cooked, quinoa clearly exceeds cooked white rice, which is often below 1 g per 100 g. It also contributes magnesium, phosphorus, manganese, and iron.

Quinoa is useful because it combines carbohydrate, good-quality protein, fiber, and micronutrients—not because it is a protein powder in grain form.

What a normal cooked serving looks like on the plate

Cooked quinoa is mostly water, so its nutrition looks much less concentrated than the dry grain. A cooked cup is roughly 185 grams and provides about 8 grams of protein, around 5 grams of fiber, and a little over 200 calories, depending on the database entry and preparation. That makes quinoa a useful whole-grain-style side dish, but not a protein food in the same category as beans, tofu, eggs, fish, or meat.

Its amino-acid profile is one reason quinoa receives attention. It supplies all essential amino acids and has relatively good lysine content compared with many cereal grains. Still, “complete protein” should not be interpreted as “high-protein.” The total grams per serving remain moderate, so a meal that needs more protein can pair quinoa with legumes, dairy, eggs, tofu, fish, or meat.

Rinsing before cooking can remove residual saponins that taste bitter or soapy on some quinoa. Many packaged products are pre-rinsed, so check the label before doing extra work. Cook it much like a small grain: use the package water ratio, simmer until the seeds are tender and the germ ring is visible, then let it rest and fluff. Texture changes substantially if too much water is used.

Compared with refined grains, quinoa can add more fiber, magnesium, phosphorus, and other minerals, but it is still a carbohydrate-rich staple. The most useful way to use it is as one component of a meal—vegetables plus quinoa plus a clear protein source—rather than expecting a bowl of quinoa alone to cover every nutritional role.

Quinoa is naturally gluten-free, but people who need strict avoidance of gluten should still look for products handled in a way that limits cross-contact with wheat, barley, or rye. This is a labeling and processing issue rather than a property of quinoa itself. For everyone else, ordinary packaged quinoa can be used much like rice or couscous in bowls, salads, soups, and side dishes.

Meal context matters for satiety. A cup of quinoa on its own supplies carbohydrate, moderate protein, and fiber; adding vegetables and a stronger protein source generally makes the meal more balanced. If calorie intake matters, remember that dry quinoa expands substantially during cooking. Measure the cooked portion rather than comparing a dry 100-gram nutrition entry with a cooked serving on your plate.

For batch cooking, cool cooked quinoa promptly and refrigerate it in a covered container. It reheats well with a splash of water and can also be used cold in salads. Treat it like other cooked grains: do not leave a large warm pot sitting out for hours. Good storage turns quinoa into a convenient base without changing its basic nutritional role.

For salads, letting cooked quinoa cool before mixing with delicate greens also keeps the vegetables from wilting and helps the grains stay separate.

faq.question: How much protein is in cooked quinoa?
faq.answer: About 4.4 g per 100 g cooked; a cooked cup around 185 g provides roughly 8 g.

faq.question: Why are dry quinoa numbers so much higher?
faq.answer: Dry quinoa contains less water. Cooking adds water and dilutes nutrients per 100 g.

faq.question: Does quinoa have more fiber than white rice?
faq.answer: Yes. Cooked quinoa is around 2.8 g per 100 g, while cooked white rice is typically below 1 g per 100 g.
